1	\section{Conclusion}
2	
3	We present the first systematic per-example analysis of attention effects in hybrid recurrent models. Per-example multiplicity spans a task-dependent variation ($\alpha = 0.14$--$0.30$) across four benchmarks, with Jaccard uniformly low ($\leq 0.10$) regardless of aggregate convergence. On LAMBADA at 1.3B, aggregate variance decreases with attention while per-example overlap saturates, consistent with configuration-specific pathways rather than uniform rescue (dependent on GDN inclusion; does not replicate on other benchmarks). Across the architectures studied here, aggregate benchmark equivalence masks per-example divergence: each backbone exhibits configuration-specific response patterns invisible to standard evaluation. Within each architecture, pure-model confidence partially predicts which examples will be affected (AUC 0.70--0.74), though disruption thresholds vary 47\% across architectures (\S\ref{ssec:per_example}).
4	
5	For practitioners, these results motivate per-example audits within the scope of controlled hybrid linear recurrent architectures studied here: the ${\sim}90\%$ non-overlap means architectures interchangeable by aggregate metrics affect largely non-overlapping examples. A majority vote across three architectures fails to consistently outperform the best individual model (LAMBADA: $-0.2$\,pp; ARC-Easy: $-1.1$\,pp; gains on other benchmarks $< 0.2$\,pp) despite 15--45\% disagreement, because roughly half of disagreement examples have only one correct architecture (Appendix~\ref{app:complementarity}). Oracle accuracy reveals $+7$--$14$\,pp of untapped complementarity, but accessing it requires selection methods beyond naive ensembling \citep{wortsman2022model}. Rescue-threshold routing extracts 36\% of oracle complementarity on LAMBADA (+5.3\,pp), demonstrating that confidence-informed selection can partially access this gap, though gains are task-dependent (\S\ref{ssec:per_example}).

39	\section*{Limitations}
40	
41	Our analysis has several limitations.
42	
43	\paragraph{Single training runs.} Each configuration corresponds to a single training run; we cannot fully disentangle architectural from seed-specific effects, though the $3\times$ within- vs.\ cross-architecture Jaccard gap (\S\ref{ssec:decoupling}) provides proxy evidence. All per-example claims are conditioned on this limitation. With $n = 5$ attention ratios, the minimum achievable $p$-value is 0.017, contributing to LAMBADA's Bonferroni-adjusted $p = .170$ not reaching conventional significance. As a partial calibration, we compare within-seed Jaccard from Pythia 70M PolyPythias \citep{vanderwal2025polypythias} against our cross-architecture values (Appendix~\ref{app:seed_calibration}); within-seed overlap is 2.7--4.3$\times$ higher, consistent with, but not definitive evidence for, architecture-driven divergence. Future work should conduct multi-seed training on matched architectures to fully isolate architectural from seed-specific effects.
44	
45	\paragraph{Coverage and generalization.} We examine three primary architectures from one model zoo on four main benchmarks (two supplementary); two additional architectures (GLA and DeltaNet) confirm the pattern at 340M (Appendix~\ref{app:extended_arch}). The controlled design isolates architectural effects but limits generalization to other hybrid families. We compare only two scale points (340M, 1.3B). Our analysis does not cover Mamba, RWKV, or generation tasks; generalization to these architectures and task types remains open.
46

ARR Responsible NLP Checklist — Draft Answers for OpenReview Submission Form
=============================================================================
Paper: "Task-Specific Convergence and Per-Example Predictive Multiplicity
        in Hybrid Recurrent Architectures"
Venue: EMNLP 2026 via ARR May/June cycle
Prepared: 2026-05-22


A. FOR EVERY SUBMISSION
========================

A1. Did you describe the limitations of your work?
Answer: Yes
Section: Limitations (after Section 5, unnumbered)
Justification: The Limitations section covers: (1) single training runs per
configuration — cannot fully disentangle architectural from seed-specific
effects, though within- vs. cross-architecture Jaccard gap (3x) and Pythia
70M seed calibration (2.7-4.3x) provide proxy evidence; (2) coverage —
five primary architectures from one model zoo, four main benchmarks + two
supplementary, two scale points only; (3) pre-training only — no fine-tuning
evaluation, discrete accuracy only; (4) statistical power — n=5 attention
ratios limits minimum achievable p to 0.017, LAMBADA Bonferroni-adjusted
p=0.170 does not reach conventional significance.

A2. Did you discuss any potential risks of your work?
Answer: Yes
Section: Ethics Statement (after Limitations)
Justification: This work analyzes existing publicly available pretrained
models and introduces no new risks. The identified per-example behavioral
differences may inform practitioners about limitations of aggregate benchmark
comparisons. No new data collection, human subjects, or model training is
involved.

A3. Do the abstract and introduction summarize the paper's main claims?
Answer: Yes
Justification: Three scoped claims: (1) task-specific aggregate convergence
(LAMBADA at 1.3B, rho=-1.0, p=0.017, with honest reporting that
Bonferroni-adjusted p=0.170); (2) scale-dependent convergence (complete at
1.3B, partial at 340M, two scale points only); (3) per-example predictive
multiplicity — pairwise Jaccard <= 0.10 across five architectures, alpha
spectrum 0.14-0.30 task-dependent. All claims explicitly scoped to the
architectures and benchmarks studied.

A4. Have you used AI writing assistants when working on this paper?
Answer: Yes
Justification: AI writing assistants were used for drafting and editing
text. All scientific content, experimental design, analysis, and claims
were verified by the authors.


B. DID YOU USE OR CREATE SCIENTIFIC ARTIFACTS?
===============================================

Answer: Yes (use existing artifacts; no new artifacts created)

B1. Did you cite the creators of artifacts you used?
Answer: Yes
Justification: We cite: Wang et al. (2025) for the hybrid architecture
model zoo (HuggingFace m-a-p organization); Gao et al. (2024) for
lm-evaluation-harness (v0.4.12); Yang et al. for flash-linear-attention
(v0.5.0); individual architecture papers for GatedDeltaNet, RetNet, HGRN2,
GLA, and DeltaNet; Marx et al. (2020) for the predictive multiplicity
framework; van der Wal et al. (2025) for PolyPythias (Pythia seed variants).
All benchmark datasets (LAMBADA, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, PIQA) are cited.

B2. Did you discuss the license or terms for use and/or distribution
    of any artifacts?
Answer: Yes
Justification: The Wang et al. model zoo is publicly released on HuggingFace.
lm-evaluation-harness is open-source under MIT license. flash-linear-attention
is open-source. All benchmark datasets are publicly available standard NLP
benchmarks. We do not release new artifacts (code release upon publication).

B3. Did you discuss if your use of existing artifact(s) was consistent
    with their intended use?
Answer: Yes
Justification: The model zoo was designed for systematic comparison of hybrid
architectures, which is exactly our use case. The evaluation harness was used
with default prompts and standard benchmark configurations.

B4. Did you discuss the steps taken to check whether the data that you
    are using/curating contains any information that names or uniquely
    identifies individual people or offensive content?
Answer: N/A
Justification: We use established NLP benchmarks (LAMBADA, ARC-Easy,
HellaSwag, PIQA) that have been widely vetted in prior work. No new data
was collected or curated.

B5. Did you provide documentation of the artifacts, e.g., coverage of
    domains, languages, and linguistic phenomena, demographic groups
    represented, etc.?
Answer: N/A
Justification: We do not release new artifacts. Analysis code and per-example
outputs will be released upon publication with documentation.

B6. Did you discuss whether and how consent was obtained from people
    whose data you're using/curating?
Answer: N/A
Justification: All data used consists of established public benchmarks.


C. DID YOU RUN COMPUTATIONAL EXPERIMENTS?
==========================================

Answer: Yes

C1. Did you report the number of parameters in the models used, the total
    computational budget (e.g., GPU hours), and computing infrastructure
    used?
Answer: Yes
Section: Section 3 (Method) and Appendix
Justification: Model sizes: 340M and 1.3B parameters. Five architectures
(GatedDeltaNet, RetNet, HGRN2, GLA, DeltaNet) x 5 attention ratios x 2
scales. All evaluation was inference-only using pretrained checkpoints from
Wang et al. (2025); no model training was performed. Computing
infrastructure: single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU. Total computational budget:
approximately 5 GPU-hours (inference only). Pythia 70M seed calibration
experiment (Appendix) used the same GPU with negligible additional compute.

C2. Did you discuss the experimental setup, including hyperparameter
    search and best model selection?
Answer: Yes
Section: Section 3
Justification: Section 3 describes the model zoo, task taxonomy (retrieval /
reasoning / mixed), all metrics (Spearman rho, cross-architecture std,
Jaccard, alpha, normalized ES), and statistical methods (permutation tests,
BCa bootstrap CIs, Bonferroni and BH corrections). All models use default
lm-evaluation-harness settings. No hyperparameter tuning or model selection
was performed — this is a post-hoc analysis of existing checkpoints.

C3. Did you report descriptive statistics about your results (e.g., error
    bars, confidence intervals, significance tests)?
Answer: Yes
Justification: We report: exact permutation tests (two-tailed, 120
permutations); BCa bootstrap confidence intervals; Bonferroni and
Benjamini-Hochberg corrections for multiple comparisons; effect sizes
(Cohen's d, Jaccard similarity, normalized ES); the ambiguity metric alpha
(Marx et al. 2020); z-scores from permutation null distributions for
Jaccard significance; Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests for
within/cross-architecture comparisons.

C4. Did you use existing packages (e.g., for pre-processing, for model
    evaluation)?
Answer: Yes
Justification: lm-evaluation-harness v0.4.12 (Gao et al. 2024) for
benchmark evaluation; flash-linear-attention v0.5.0 for efficient linear
attention inference; PyTorch; standard scientific Python stack (numpy, scipy,
scikit-learn for statistical tests).


D. DID YOU USE HUMAN ANNOTATORS (E.G., CROWDWORKERS) OR INVOLVE HUMAN
   PARTICIPANTS?
==========================================

Answer: No

D1-D5: N/A
Justification: No human annotation or human participants were involved.
This is a purely computational analysis of existing pretrained models on
established benchmarks.


E. DID YOU USE AI ASSISTANTS (E.G., CHATGPT)?
===============================================

E1. Did you report the use of AI assistants (e.g., ChatGPT, Copilot)?
Answer: Yes
Justification: See A4. AI writing assistants were used for drafting and
editing. All scientific content was verified by the authors.


ADDITIONAL NOTES FOR FORM FIELDS
=================================

Fairness / Bias Implications (if asked):
Per-example predictive multiplicity has direct fairness implications.
Different architectures with equivalent aggregate performance affect nearly
disjoint sets of examples (Jaccard <= 0.10, ~90% non-overlap). This means
the choice of architecture — often made based on aggregate benchmarks alone
— determines WHICH specific examples are correctly or incorrectly predicted.
The ambiguity metric alpha ranges from 0.14 (reasoning tasks) to 0.30
(retrieval tasks), quantifying the fraction of examples whose predictions
depend on architecture choice. This is an instance of predictive multiplicity
(Marx et al. 2020) arising from architectural variation, complementing
underspecification (D'Amour et al. 2022) which focuses on same-pipeline
variation. Practitioners should be aware that aggregate-equivalent models
are not per-example equivalent.

Reproducibility:
All models are publicly available from the Wang et al. (2025) model zoo on
HuggingFace (m-a-p organization). Evaluation uses the standard
lm-evaluation-harness with default settings. Analysis code and per-example
outputs will be released upon publication. No training is required to
reproduce results — only inference on public checkpoints.
